claim: Creative and multimedia work accounts for about 74% of Indonesia's online workforce and 47% of the Philippines', having risen 40 and 34 percentage points respectively across 2017-2020 -- so Southeast Asia's digital labour force is disproportionately concentrated in exactly the low-bargaining-power creative occupations.
stance_target: The claim that Southeast Asian digital creative work is structurally different in composition from Western digital work and cannot be analysed with Western occupational assumptions
scope_conditions: Oxford Internet Institute Online Labour Index data 2017-2020; covers online freelancing platforms (Upwork/Freelancer type), NOT social media content creation; PIDS discussion paper self-labelled preliminary, unedited and unreviewed
quoted_support: From 2017-2020, the share of these workers has increased by 34 and 40 percentage points in Bangladesh and Indonesia, respectively. To date, it accounts for around 59% and 74% of Bangladesh and Indonesia's online workforce, respectively. In the Philippines, the share of creative and multimedia online workers is the highest (47%)

claim: Crowdworkers in North America, Europe and Central Asia earn more than those in Africa and Asia-Pacific for equivalent online work, and non-Western workers are systematically poorly rewarded -- a documented geographic earnings penalty independent of skill.
stance_target: The transferability of Western creator and digital-worker income benchmarks to Southeast Asia
scope_conditions: Online freelancing platforms; citing Berg et al (2018) ILO Survey of Crowdworkers and Beerepoot and Lambregts (2014); secondary citation within a preliminary PIDS discussion paper; specific magnitudes not given here
quoted_support: Initial evidence shows that crowdworkers in Northern America, Europe, and Central Asia earn more than those in Africa and Asia and the Pacific (see Berg et al, 2018) and that non-western workers could be poorly rewarded in online work (Beerepoot and Lambregts, 2014).
numbers: magnitudes not stated in this source
region: Global, comparing Asia-Pacific to North America and Europe

claim: Structural labour oversupply drives down Southeast Asian digital-work compensation: the Philippines alone accounts for 12% of global oversupply on one major platform, pushing workers to underbid each other and eliminating individual bargaining power.
stance_target: The claim that per-worker income in Southeast Asian digital work is set by supply-side competition rather than by demand growth, so a growing market does not imply growing per-creator income
scope_conditions: One unnamed major online labour platform; figure presented in Table 2 of a preliminary PIDS discussion paper; online freelancing, not content creation
quoted_support: In one platform, evidence shows that the Philippines accounts for 12% of the global oversupply (table 2). Not only will oversupply exert a downward pressure on compensation as workers potentially underbid each other but this will adversely affect the workers' bargaining power as well.
numbers: demand: North America 47%, Europe 24%, Asia 19%, US alone 40%

claim: Reintermediation creates a hidden second tier of digital workers: successful online workers subcontract work to less visible, less experienced workers at lower compensation, so platform-visible earnings overstate what the bottom tier actually receives.
stance_target: The claim that platform-observable earnings data systematically misses the lowest-paid participants, biasing measured income distributions upward
scope_conditions: Online freelancing platforms, Philippines and Asian context, 2020; qualitative observation in a preliminary discussion paper, not quantified
quoted_support: which successful online workers are taking on work that they farm out to other less visible and less experienced online workers, can lead to exploitation

claim: Southeast Asian platform workers are young and largely without social protection: average age 31 in the Philippines and 33 globally, with only around 60% holding health insurance and 35% a pension per the 2015 ILO Survey of Crowdworkers, and 70% unable to access maternity, childcare or housing protections per Forde et al (2017).
stance_target: The claim that digital self-employment in Southeast Asia carries no institutional safety net, which shapes both who enters and when they must exit
scope_conditions: 2015 ILO Survey of Crowdworkers (Berg et al 2018) and a 2017 five-platform survey (Forde et al 2017); Philippine age figure from the 2020 PIDS-DICT Online Survey of Market and Non-Market Work; crowdworkers not content creators
quoted_support: based on the 2015 ILO Survey of Crowdworkers, only around 60% were covered by health insurance and around 35% had a pension plan (Berg et al, 2018). In a survey of five major platforms in 2017, Forde et al (2017) find that only around 36% are subscribed into a personal pension while 70% could not access protections such as maternity, childcare, and housing
numbers: 25-year-old 8pp more likely to be a platform worker than a 35-year-old

claim: A Philippine government think-tank paper devoted to online work reports no median or mean earnings figure, no attrition rate and no survival data for Philippine online workers -- an audited absence in the highest-authority SEA source located.
stance_target: The claim that quantitative income-distribution and attrition evidence for Southeast Asian digital work does not exist even in official statistical and think-tank literature
scope_conditions: PIDS Discussion Paper 2020-29, December 2020; verified by full-text search of the document for earnings, median, average and attrition figures
quoted_support: The PIDS Discussion Paper Series constitutes studies that are preliminary and subject to further revisions ... The studies under the Series are unedited and unreviewed.
